newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-German M3 overshoots 1996 goal, rates held.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German M3 overshoots 1996 goal, rates held.

text.p: The Bundesbank said on Thursday that growth in German M3 money supply slowed marginally in December, but admitted that its main monetary policy indicator had grown far beyond target in 1996.
The German central bank said M3 grew at an annualised rate of 7.9 percent in December compared with its average level in the final quarter of 1995.

It grew by 8.1 percent in the final quarter of 1996 from the final quarter a year earlier. The Bundesbank had set a four to seven percent expansion corridor for money supply growth between the fourth quarter of 1995 and final quarter of 1996.
"In the entire fourth quarter of 1996 (M3 money supply) was 8.1 percent higher than in the fourth quarter 1995," the Bundesbank said.
"The money supply target for 1996, which looked for an expansion of M3 by four to seven percent in this period, was therefore overstepped," it added.
News that the central bank had overshot its target came as no surprise to financial markets, after double-digit growth rates early last year failed to slow as quickly as the Bundesbank had hoped.

The central bank, which blamed uncertainty in bond markets throughout much of last year as a major factor in buoying M3 growth, acknowledged several months ago that its 1996 target had slipped out of reach.

But German debt prices slipped on the back of the firmer than expected December M3 figure. Bonds later recovered to trade moderately higher after the central bank, as expected, left interest rates unchanged at its regular policy meeting.
The German discount rate was left at 2.50 percent and the Lombard rate at 4.50 percent. The central bank's repo rate was also held at three percent.

Economists had generally expected the Bundesbank to leave credit costs unchanged at the meeting, although there was a growing view that the central bank could lower the repo rate at a meeting later in the first or second quarter.

These hopes were reinforced by December's M3 growth data, which pointed to a sharp slowdown in the headline figure in January. The continued strong growth in M3 in the final month of 1996 means the base for next year's target will be high.
Due to statistical effects, M3 growth is therefore likely to look weak in the early months of 1997. The Bundesbank has set a target of 3-1/2 to 6-1/2 percent growth for 1997.
Keith Edmonds, chief analyst at IBJ International in London said weak growth could give the Bundesbank the excuse it needs to justify a rate cut to help the weak economy.
"M3 growth was very strong in first half of last year so as a result the January figure will come in at a very low figure. The Bundesbank will use that as an excuse to cut interest rates."
Michael Hochguertel at BHF-Bank in Frankfurt agreed, saying: "The question is where M3 will be at the start of next year and I'd expect a rather low figure due to statistical effects."
Hochguertel said the January growth figure was likely to be within or even below the 1997 growth target, adding that this could provide the basis for a small interest rate cut.

But Juergen Stanowsky, an economist at Dresdner Bank in Frankfurt, who also believed January M3 would be at the lower end of the new target range, said he did not expect this to lead to an interest rate cut.

"I don't think rates will come down. The total value of the D-mark has come down. This will boost exports. So I would not paint a Doomsday picture. I don't think there are domestic reasons for the Bundesbank to cut rates," he said.
